segments.title: A great-power fleet beyond Free French reach
segments.body: France entered World War II with one of the world's great navies. Free French forces inherited that naval identity while having access to only part of the fleet. Ships became available at different times, making it difficult to assemble their full capability. Their wartime duties also differed from the missions for which they had been designed, although some designs, especially the large destroyers, adapted well.

evidence.note: The French Navy's great-power standing, limited Free French access to its fleet, staggered availability, and differences between intended and actual wartime missions.

segments.summary: Free French naval ambitions depended on which ships became available and how well those ships adapted to a different war.

segments.title: Which French ships did the Royal Navy miss most?
segments.body: French large destroyers rank highest in this assessment of the capability the Royal Navy lost when much of the French fleet ceased fighting alongside it. They offered the closest Allied counterpart to the Tribal class in the Atlantic and Mediterranean. Their surface-combat strength made them useful whenever they became available. The timing of that availability determined whether the Allies could use them when they were most needed.

evidence.note: French large destroyers rank highest in the assessment of missing French capabilities, with the Tribal class as their closest Allied comparison in the Atlantic and Mediterranean.

segments.summary: French large destroyers supplied a scarce counterpart to Tribal-class combat power, making their absence especially costly.
segments.question: What did the Royal Navy miss most when much of the French Navy was absent from Allied operations in World War II?
segments.answerShort: French large destroyers, judged here the most valuable missing capability because they were the closest Allied counterpart to the Tribal class in the Atlantic and Mediterranean.

segments.title: Contre-torpilleurs in task-group doctrine
segments.body: French interwar planning built around mixed task groups of capital ships, cruisers, and destroyers. In the British planning rationale outlined here, only a war with the United States would require the whole fleet. Other wars called for mixed formations, each needing enough cruisers to support it. France faced the same shortage and turned earlier to large, fast destroyers for scouting and surface combat. These contre-torpilleurs exceeded 2,000 tons standard displacement in the 1920s, before the British Tribal class. Later French designs were intended to defeat small Italian Condottieri-type cruisers and scouts, making their absence from Allied Mediterranean operations especially significant.

evidence.note: British and French mixed task-group planning, the British expectation that only a US war would require the whole fleet, cruiser requirements, and France's use of large fast destroyers to address a cruiser shortage.
Contre-torpilleurs served as scouts and heavily armed destroyers exceeding 2,000 tons standard displacement in the 1920s.
Later French large destroyers were intended to defeat Italian scout cruisers, with a comparison to Tribal-class wartime operations.

segments.summary: French interwar doctrine used large contre-torpilleurs to give mixed task groups scouting power and enough gun strength to challenge Italian light cruisers.

segments.title: Léopard's training service and changing weapons
segments.body: The Chacal class was an early, mildly experimental contre-torpilleur design that still produced capable ships. Léopard served with other members of the class before transferring with Chacal to the École Navale at Brest in 1935. Her 75 mm guns were replaced by four twin 13.2 mm anti-aircraft machine-gun mounts. The criticism of that change is explicitly made with hindsight: the machine guns required aircraft to come much closer. Early in 1940, Léopard received Asdic and had her previously removed depth charges restored for anti-submarine work.

evidence.note: The early Chacal-class design and Léopard's squadron service and 1935 move to the naval school at Brest.
Replacement of 75 mm guns with 13.2 mm machine guns, criticized with hindsight for their short effective reach.
Asdic installation and restoration of depth charges early in 1940.

segments.summary: Léopard's prewar training career and armament changes show a Chacal-class destroyer preparing for the anti-aircraft and anti-submarine demands of war.

segments.title: Léopard's Channel fighting and the need for a staff ship
segments.body: Léopard served with Western Maritime Forces Command and came under Admiral Abrial in May 1940. She supported Dunkirk and Cherbourg, fired on advancing German forces, and helped lead groups of smaller torpilleurs d'escadre. An admiral commanded the wider force from an aviso, whose accommodation could house his staff. Even large French destroyers lacked the limited staff space available in comparable British destroyers, so hull size alone did not make them suitable flagships. Léopard fired some of the last shots around Boulogne-sur-Mer on 24 May and later rescued 19 mainly British soldiers from a sinking boat, carrying them to England.

evidence.note: Channel duties under Admiral Abrial, leadership of smaller destroyers, and the use of an aviso for an admiral and staff.
Gunfire around Boulogne-sur-Mer on 24 May, Dunkirk operations, and the rescue of 19 mainly British soldiers.

segments.summary: Coastal gunfire and a small rescue formed part of Léopard's Channel service, while an aviso supplied the staff accommodation her destroyer force lacked.

segments.title: Léopard's Free French commander and wartime pseudonym
segments.body: France's fall found Léopard at Portsmouth, where Operation Catapult placed her under British control. She was quickly handed to the Free French. Jules Evenou received command and served under a nom de guerre. Free French personnel used assumed names to protect their families, linking a command appointment at sea to the risks their relatives faced at home.

evidence.note: Léopard's seizure at Portsmouth, rapid transfer to the Free French, Jules Evenou's command, and the use of noms de guerre to protect families.

segments.summary: Léopard's early transfer to the Free French brought Jules Evenou to command under an assumed wartime name intended to protect his family.

segments.title: Léopard's British rearmament and uncertain submarine claim
segments.body: British modifications replaced two of Léopard's after 13.2 mm mounts with a 4-inch gun between the funnels. The forward machine-gun mounts moved higher on the superstructure and two 2-pounder pom-poms were added. She then joined Western Approaches convoy escort duty and rescued 39 survivors from a cargo vessel. An archived account of her commander's service also credited five attacks on a German submarine and a probable sinking. Its translated wording calls these grenade attacks, probably meaning depth-charge attacks. The original French version could not be checked through the archive, so both the translation problem and the uncertainty of the sinking claim remain.

evidence.note: British changes to the 13.2 mm mounts, addition of a 4-inch gun and pom-poms, Western Approaches convoy duty, and rescue of 39 survivors.
An archived translated account credits five grenade attacks and a probable submarine sinking. Depth charges are the presumed meaning, and access problems prevented checking the original French text.

segments.summary: British weapons strengthened Léopard for Atlantic escort work, but a translated account leaves uncertainty over a claimed submarine sinking.

segments.title: Trading Léopard's speed for fuel, depth charges, and radar
segments.body: Léopard's escort conversion removed the forward boiler and funnel to make room for fuel and additional accommodation. Top speed fell to 31.5 knots, while range increased to about 4,200 nautical miles at 15 knots and accommodation rose to a maximum of 234 men. Depth-charge rails replaced the unsatisfactory chutes and allowed heavier charges to be carried. Throwers added to the anti-submarine fit. Oerlikons replaced the 4-inch gun and more pom-poms strengthened the medium and light anti-aircraft battery. The reduced topweight made room for Type 291 search radar, adapting the ship more closely to ocean escort work.

evidence.note: Boiler and funnel removal, 31.5-knot speed, 4,200-nautical-mile range at 15 knots, and accommodation for up to 234 men.
Depth-charge rails and throwers, heavier charges, revised light anti-aircraft armament, and topweight capacity for Type 291 search radar.

segments.summary: Léopard exchanged a boiler and some speed for greater endurance, heavier depth charges, extra accommodation, and Type 291 radar.

segments.title: Léopard and the liberation of La Réunion
segments.body: Léopard arrived off La Réunion in November 1942 carrying 80 soldiers. The landing force took Saint-Denis while the governor withdrew into the island's interior. A coastal battery resisted and exchanged fire with the destroyer, causing deaths on both sides. The island surrendered on 30 November. She then patrolled the Indian Ocean until March 1943.

evidence.note: Arrival with 80 soldiers, capture of Saint-Denis, combat with a coastal battery, surrender on 30 November 1942, and subsequent Indian Ocean patrols.

segments.summary: Léopard's intervention at La Réunion combined troop transport, an amphibious landing, coastal gunfire, and the political recovery of the island for Free France.

segments.title: Tigre's long war with few opportunities
segments.body: Tigre escaped Mers-el-Kebir after she and Lynx briefly engaged HMS Wrestler and depth-charged HMS Proteus. Vichy reserve service left her stripped of armament, and the Germans captured her at Toulon before transferring her to Italy. As FR 23 she served mainly as a transport. The Free French took custody at Bizerte in October 1943 and recommissioned her in December, but repairs delayed her return to service until March 1944. Oerlikons strengthened her light anti-aircraft armament before near-miss damage in 1944 led to further work. An escort conversion improved her fuel capacity and accommodation and replaced her depth-charge arrangements. She escorted convoys and supported the Allied flank force along the Italian-French border. After the war she ferried troops, supported French forces in Algeria, and served as a gunnery and then engineering training ship. A long career gave her fewer wartime opportunities than Léopard's shorter period of intense activity.

evidence.note: Tigre's Mers-el-Kebir escape and combat, capture at Toulon, Italian service as FR 23, October 1943 handover at Bizerte, and return to service in March 1944.
Poor material condition, Oerlikon additions, near-miss damage in 1944, escort conversion, convoy work, and gunfire support for the Allied flank force.
Postwar troop transport, Algeria support, gunnery and engineering training, and the contrast with Léopard's shorter active career.

segments.summary: Tigre was a capable Chacal-class destroyer, but Mers-el-Kebir, Vichy reserve status, Italian custody, and late repair kept her from useful Allied service until 1944.

segments.title: Le Fantasque and the cruiser-destroyer boundary
segments.body: France and Italy approached the same high-speed surface-combat problem from opposite directions: France built very large destroyers while Italy favored very small cruisers. Le Fantasque-class ships displaced about 2,569 tons standard and roughly 3,400 tons at deep load, close to the cruiser boundary. Their five 5.5-inch guns and nine torpedoes in three triple mountings gave them a strong surface-action fit. Their stability allowed them to work the guns, although the rate of fire remained modest. Official top speed was 37 knots, with about 45 knots achieved by some ships on trials and nearly matched by others in wartime operations. Light anti-aircraft weapons included 37 mm guns and twin 13.2 mm machine guns, and wartime complement reached 265.

evidence.note: French large-destroyer and Italian small-cruiser approaches, with standard and deep-load displacements for Le Fantasque.
Five 5.5-inch guns, stability and rate-of-fire limits, official and trial speeds, nine torpedoes, light anti-aircraft weapons, and a wartime crew of 265.

segments.summary: The Le Fantasque class pushed the French large-destroyer idea close to the cruiser boundary with very high speed, five 5.5-inch guns, and nine torpedoes.

segments.title: Le Fantasque's gun elevation and ammunition limits
segments.body: Le Fantasque's main guns elevated only to 30 degrees. Higher-angle mountings for weapons of this size would have required much more space. The ammunition figure is corrected during the explanation to 200 rounds per gun, giving 1,000 main-battery rounds, plus 75 star shells overall. A large ammunition supply did not remove the guns' limited rate of fire. All six ships were completed, making this the last fully built contre-torpilleur class before the war, while only two of the later Mogadors reached completion.

evidence.note: Thirty-degree maximum elevation, the space needed for higher-angle mounts, 200 rounds per gun, the correction to 75 star shells overall, and modest rate of fire.
All six Le Fantasque-class ships were completed before the war, followed by only two Mogadors.

segments.summary: Low gun elevation, mounting space, and a modest rate of fire constrained a destroyer battery carrying 1,000 main rounds and 75 star shells overall.

segments.title: Machinery trouble brings Le Triomphant to the Free French
segments.body: Le Triomphant took part in an operation to intercept German merchant ships bound for Norway. The force fought German torpedo boats, but heavy seas probably caused more of her damage than the engagement. Engine problems forced her to stop at Plymouth for repairs. Her presence there allowed Operation Catapult to bring her under British control, followed quickly by transfer to the Free French. She became one of their largest available modern warships, and her wartime modifications included Asdic and British radar fitted in an American yard.

evidence.note: British radar fitted in an American yard, Asdic, the Norway-bound merchant interception, probable sea damage, Plymouth repairs, and transfer through Operation Catapult to the Free French.

segments.summary: Engine trouble left Le Triomphant at Plymouth during Operation Catapult, making a modern large destroyer available to the Free French.

segments.title: Why high speed in heavy seas damaged destroyer turbines
segments.body: Le Triomphant's recurring machinery faults resemble the Tribal class's turbine problems in this diagnosis. A large destroyer could keep driving through heavy seas while its relatively light machinery absorbed repeated shocks. Those shocks unseat turbine blades and produce accumulating damage during prolonged high-speed operation. Ships below roughly 3,000 tons standard displacement are identified as particularly exposed under those conditions. The comparison with contemporary Western warships around 6,000 tons concerns their room for larger machinery and gearing able to withstand sustained strain. Displacement, machinery weight, and intended cruising speed therefore have to be considered together.

evidence.note: A comparison with Tribal-class turbineitis links heavy-sea shocks to displaced turbine blades and contrasts small destroyer machinery with larger modern installations.

segments.summary: Le Triomphant's machinery problems are compared with Tribal-class turbine damage caused by sustained high speed and repeated shocks in heavy seas.

segments.title: Le Triomphant's Pacific patrols and ten-month Sydney refit
segments.body: Le Triomphant's Panama Canal transit was reported so accurately that it revealed Japanese observation of passing ships. She visited French Polynesia, Fiji, and other Pacific islands as a Free French presence, then suffered damage between New Zealand and Sydney. Evacuation and escort duties followed. A refit at Garden Island Dockyard in Sydney lasted from March 1942 to January 1943 because compatible French spare parts were difficult to obtain. Unfamiliar machinery had to be rebuilt, leaving an otherwise useful warship unavailable during the Japanese advances.

evidence.note: Japanese observation of the Panama Canal transit, Pacific island visits, damage on passage to Sydney, evacuations, and escort work.
The March 1942 to January 1943 Garden Island refit, spare-part shortages, and the need to rebuild unfamiliar French machinery.

segments.summary: Pacific patrols, evacuations, and escort work repeatedly gave way to repairs, including a long Sydney refit caused by missing French spare parts.

segments.title: Le Triomphant's cruiser label and worldwide repair cycle
segments.body: Le Triomphant returned to escort duties that included supporting iron-ore shipping routes. American officials resisted treating Le Triomphant as a destroyer, while the French continued to regard her as a contre-torpilleur. Her nominal reclassification as a light cruiser is dated either during or after a Sydney refit between September and November 1943, with French acceptance limited. After taking aboard a Royal Australian Navy liaison team, she accompanied an American oil tanker toward the Mediterranean. Damage forced the tanker to tow her, and a typhoon caused further harm. HMS Frobisher helped her onward to Diego Suarez in French Madagascar. Temporary repairs there benefited from facilities working in the same language as her manuals. Full restoration in Boston lasted until April 1945, after which she joined the Royal Navy's Eastern Fleet in the Indian Ocean. Repairs had consumed much of her war despite her usefulness whenever she was operational.

evidence.note: Escort duties and an American-French classification dispute, with uncertainty over whether light-cruiser reclassification occurred during or after the September to November 1943 refit.
Australian liaison personnel, tanker towing, typhoon damage, help from HMS Frobisher, repairs at Diego Suarez and Boston, and late Eastern Fleet service.

segments.summary: Arguments over whether Le Triomphant was a destroyer or light cruiser accompanied a repair cycle that stretched from Sydney through Diego Suarez to Boston.

segments.title: La Terrible from Mers-el-Kebir to Corsica
segments.body: La Terrible began the war with Force de Raid amid French Atlantic operations that included the search for Admiral Graf Spee. During the British attack at Mers-el-Kebir, she escaped with Strasbourg and engaged Royal Navy destroyers on the way to Toulon. Later Vichy maintenance left her in unusually good condition when Operation Torch brought her into the Allied camp. Upgraded Asdic and radar then supported a useful career that included visits to Martinique and Algeria and the landing of personnel on Corsica. Her anti-aircraft armament was not upgraded at that stage.

evidence.note: Force de Raid service, French Atlantic operations, escape from Mers-el-Kebir with Strasbourg, and the return to the North African base.
Good condition after Vichy maintenance, Allied acquisition after Operation Torch, Asdic and radar upgrades, and subsequent visits to Martinique and Algeria and landings on Corsica.

segments.summary: La Terrible served with Force de Raid in Atlantic operations, escaped Mers-el-Kebir, and entered Allied service after Operation Torch for work in the West Indies, North Africa, and Corsica.

segments.title: How naval treaties pushed destroyers toward cruiser roles
segments.body: La Terrible and her sisters were sometimes reclassified as light cruisers because their size and firepower exceeded familiar destroyer categories. One counterfactual proposal is that large destroyers would have become a normal type without the treaty system, with separate large and small destroyer lines. In that proposed development, smaller destroyers and sloops move toward escort and frigate duties while larger destroyers absorb some light-cruiser functions. Cruisers could then concentrate on more demanding roles. The accompanying criticism of naval treaties is that restrictions on capital ships and carriers pushed other categories to grow in size to undertake their missions.

evidence.note: The destroyer-versus-light-cruiser dispute and the counterfactual suggestion that large and small destroyer lines would have developed without the treaty system.
The argument that treaty restrictions on capital ships and carriers pushed smaller categories to grow so they could undertake additional missions.

segments.summary: The disputed classification of large French destroyers raises a counterfactual about separate destroyer and frigate lines and an argument about treaty-driven growth.

segments.title: La Terrible as a useful but late Allied asset
segments.body: La Terrible performed useful Allied work and sank several ships once the opportunity came. The limiting factor was timing: by 1943 the peak crises in the Atlantic and Mediterranean were beginning to recede. Sending her to the Far East would have aggravated an already difficult support problem for French machinery. Keeping her near North African French bases made sustainment easier and released other Allied ships for distant work. That practical choice reduced her opportunities for major fleet action.

evidence.note: La Terrible's useful Allied operations and ship sinkings, with availability in 1943 after the peak Atlantic and Mediterranean crises.
Access to French support facilities in North Africa favored keeping the ship in the Atlantic area, where she could release other Allied units for distant service.

segments.summary: La Terrible could relieve other Allied ships after 1943, but she arrived after the hardest Atlantic and Mediterranean fighting and had to remain near French support facilities.

segments.title: Why the Bourrasque class's ordinary utility mattered
segments.body: French doctrine paired large contre-torpilleurs with smaller torpilleurs d'escadre, while avisos covered duties comparable to British sloops. The twelve Bourrasque-class ships supplied dependable fleet-destroyer numbers at roughly 1,300 tons standard displacement. Their balance of qualities included 33-knot speed, about 2,000 nautical miles of range at 14 knots, four 5-inch guns, and six torpedoes. Fleets needed ships that could perform ordinary escort and fleet duties alongside designs built for exceptional performance. The Polish Wicher class drew on the same basic design. Comparison with the Royal Navy's W class supports the preference for a proven balance of qualities, with reservations about the choice of 13.2 mm anti-aircraft machine guns.

evidence.note: Torpilleurs d'escadre and avisos within French force structure, twelve Bourrasque-class ships, their displacement, speed, range, torpedoes, guns, and light anti-aircraft weapons.
The Polish Wicher class's design relationship and a comparison with British W-class destroyers support the case for balanced, dependable fleet ships.

segments.summary: The smaller torpilleurs d'escadre supplied numbers and dependable fleet work alongside the faster, more heavily armed contre-torpilleurs.

segments.title: Operation Catapult and government war preparedness
segments.body: A damaged French destroyer was towed from Brest to Devonport and repaired, but she had little crew aboard when Operation Catapult brought her under British control. Britain feared the consequences of French warships in its ports coming under hostile authority after the French government's collapse. The criticism of Allied planning is that too few contingencies had been agreed for such a rupture. Even with advance planning, the divided and changing French political response might have frustrated those arrangements. In this interpretation, the collapse was chiefly governmental, rather than simply the collapse of the army or nation. Strategic preparation therefore needed to include government structures and procedures for setbacks as well as plans for military operations.

evidence.note: A damaged destroyer's tow from Brest to Devonport, completed repairs, a limited crew, and British concerns about control of French warships during Operation Catapult.
Criticism of Allied contingency planning and French governmental collapse, qualified by doubt that advance planning would have solved the problem, followed by the case for government preparedness.

segments.summary: Operation Catapult raises the problem of preparing governments and alliances for military setbacks, divided authority, and uncertainty over control of warships.

segments.title: A Polish-crewed Bourrasque-class destroyer without spares
segments.body: A Bourrasque-class destroyer sailed under a Polish ensign from July 1940 to April 1941, using a designation meaning French ship instead of the usual ORP prefix. Most of her crew came from Grom, lost around Narvik in May 1940. Her duties included escorts, raids, and convoy support. Storm damage flooded an engine, while compatible French spare parts remained scarce. Nearly 200 of roughly 300 days under Polish control were spent under repair. The Free French later passed her to the Royal Navy in 1943 because they could not keep her operational. Evacuating a hull without sufficient spares saved the ship but left its new operators unable to sustain it.

evidence.note: Polish service from July 1940 to April 1941, a French-ship designation instead of ORP, a largely Grom-derived crew, operational duties, storm damage, and nearly 200 of roughly 300 days under repair. The Free French later passed her to the Royal Navy in 1943.
The need to include adequate spare parts when evacuating ships from French ports.

segments.summary: A Bourrasque-class destroyer transferred to the Free Polish Navy shows how an available hull could still be immobilized by storm damage and missing French spare parts.

segments.title: Mistral from partial scuttling to Normandy
segments.body: Mistral served under Guillaume Christophe Marie Pons, Count of Toulouse-Lautrec Montfa. She had already taken part in the Dunkirk evacuation when he tried to scuttle her during Operation Catapult. The attempt only partly succeeded, so the British repaired and rearmed her with Royal Navy guns. Distrust of the original crew and scarce Free French manpower led the Royal Navy to operate her as HMS Mistral. Escort duty ended in a collision with the tanker Black Ranger and another repair period. She returned to the Free French in time for Normandy, where German coastal artillery damaged her badly enough to make her a constructive total loss. Political distrust, crew scarcity, and damage repeatedly interrupted her service.

evidence.note: Dunkirk service, partial scuttling during Operation Catapult, British repair and rearmament, distrust of the original crew, and limited Free French manpower. The rearmament wording is unclear about the gun count and calibre.
Escort duty, collision with Black Ranger, repairs, return to the Free French for Normandy, and disabling German coastal-artillery damage.

segments.summary: Mistral's partial scuttling led to British control and rearmament before she finally returned to the Free French for Normandy support and was disabled by coastal artillery.

segments.title: Toulouse-Lautrec Montfa and divided French loyalties
segments.body: Mistral's commander had worked extensively with the Royal Navy before choosing Vichy service. His professional ties to Britain make that choice surprising in this assessment, although his determination to prevent British seizure of his ship is treated as understandable. He later served successfully within the Vichy structure and participated in rebuilding the French Navy. In 1946 he was a liaison officer with British naval forces in Germany. His wartime allegiance did not end his professional relationship with Britain.

evidence.note: The commander's resistance to British seizure, the surprising choice of Vichy service despite Royal Navy ties, and later French naval reconstruction and liaison work with British naval forces in Germany in 1946.

segments.summary: Toulouse-Lautrec Montfa chose Vichy service despite close Royal Navy ties, then renewed those ties through liaison work after the war.

segments.title: L'Adroit as workhorse design and Dunkirk loss
segments.body: The L'Adroit class continued the torpilleur d'escadre role as a fleet workhorse, with six torpedoes and a gun fit broadly similar to the preceding smaller destroyers. L'Adroit herself supported the northern coastal flank and the Dunkirk evacuation under Henry Dupin de Saint-Cyran. Heinkel He 111 bombers damaged the ship, forcing him to beach her at Malo-les-Bains. A later forward-magazine explosion tore open the hull and left her unusable, while all the crew survived in safe positions. Deliberate detonation to deny the stranded ship to German forces is suggested as a possible explanation. The cause remains uncertain.

evidence.note: The L'Adroit class's fleet-destroyer role, six torpedoes, and a fit broadly similar to the preceding smaller destroyers.
Henry Dupin de Saint-Cyran's command, coastal and Dunkirk operations, He 111 bombing, beaching at Malo-les-Bains, and a disabling magazine explosion survived by the whole crew.
The explicitly tentative suggestion that the forward magazine was detonated to deny the stranded ship to the enemy.

segments.summary: The L'Adroit class continued France's practical fleet-destroyer line, while the lead ship's bombing, beaching, and magazine explosion show the violence of the Dunkirk campaign.

segments.title: Alcyon and Basque enter Allied service late
segments.body: Alcyon fought for Vichy France at Casablanca before the North African capitulation brought her into Allied service. Modernization allowed her to continue useful work through the war and beyond, until withdrawal from service in 1948. Basque had remained at Alexandria after Operation Catapult and rejoined the Allied forces in July 1943. Both ships had useful capabilities that the Allies lacked while they were unavailable.

evidence.note: Alcyon's Vichy service at Casablanca, transfer after the North African capitulation, modernization, Allied work, and withdrawal in 1948.
Basque's presence at Alexandria during Operation Catapult and return to Allied service in July 1943, followed by the question of what earlier availability could have contributed.

segments.summary: Alcyon's Vichy service at Casablanca and Basque's detention at Alexandria delayed their contribution to the Allied war effort.

segments.title: What a mass French fleet escape might have changed
segments.body: A mass departure of French ships in 1940 could have given the Allies a major early increase in naval strength. The counterfactual includes ships outside France and others able to escape, carrying as many troops and other personnel as possible. That departure would also have deprived Vichy France of a major asset. The dilemma is that keeping the fleet outside Allied operations also benefited the Axis, even while the ships remained outside direct Axis control.

evidence.note: The counterfactual of a mass French fleet departure with troops and personnel, its potential value to the Allies, and Vichy's loss of an asset whose absence from Allied service benefited the Axis.

segments.summary: A mass escape of ships and personnel could have strengthened the Allies while depriving Vichy France of a major asset.

segments.title: La Combattante's Hunt-class service at Normandy
segments.body: La Combattante began as Haldon, a Type III Hunt-class destroyer. Under Free French operation she spent much of the war on convoy duties and also carried out fire-support missions. A humorous signal associated with her Normandy grounding celebrates a French ship being first to touch French soil. Under Commander André Patou, her confident crew combined convoy escort work with direct support for the land campaign.

evidence.note: Haldon and Type III Hunt-class origins, convoy and fire-support work, the Normandy grounding, and André Patou's command. The narration attributes the humorous signal to La Combattante.

segments.summary: A British-built Hunt became a Free French convoy escort and fire-support ship, with a humorous signal after grounding during the Normandy campaign.

segments.title: La Combattante carries de Gaulle and French currency to Normandy
segments.body: La Combattante carried Charles de Gaulle and other senior officers to Normandy in 1944. Commander André Patou inferred the destination even though he had not received the orders, prompting an exchange in which he assured de Gaulle that the ship already knew the way. The mission also carried a fund of 250 million francs. The Free French government feared that American-issued notes would displace the French franc in ordinary circulation. Delivering French notes with senior officials able to authorize their use was intended to preserve French monetary control as territory was liberated. The financial concern was that displacing the existing franc could cause hyperinflation and force a rebuilding of the currency system.

evidence.note: De Gaulle's voyage with senior officers and the exchange with André Patou about orders and the destination. The narration dates the voyage to July 1944.
The 250-million-franc fund, Free French concern over American-issued notes becoming the circulating currency, and the stated risks to the existing franc and economy.

segments.summary: The voyage combined the return of French political leaders with a currency delivery intended to maintain French monetary authority in liberated territory.

segments.title: La Combattante's mine loss and the rejected torpedo claim
segments.body: La Combattante's active service depended on keeping her in good material condition. A mine sank her on 23 February 1945. Two motor torpedo boats rescued 118 of the crew, while 67 were lost. The German torpedo claim is rejected because the vessel credited with sinking her had actually sunk a British cable layer. The mine's exact type remains disputed, with an air-dropped mine mentioned as a possibility.

evidence.note: Maintained condition and active service, the 23 February 1945 mine loss, rescue and casualty figures, the conflicting German claim, and uncertainty over an air-dropped mine.

segments.summary: La Combattante was lost to a mine, with 118 rescued and 67 dead. A German torpedo claim concerned a different victim.

segments.title: Could a larger Free French fleet have supported itself?
segments.body: A larger Free French fleet would have offered the Allies more useful ships. Supporting them without access to France's domestic supply and maintenance systems would still have been a logistical problem. One open possibility is that a larger early transfer might also have brought more sustainment infrastructure, including French North African facilities. A second question concerns how the destroyers would have performed if more had been available for the tactical roles intended before the war. These counterfactuals remain open for consideration.

evidence.note: More ships are weighed against support and maintenance problems, with the open possibility that a larger Free French force would also have brought French North African infrastructure.
The unanswered counterfactual about more French destroyers operating in their intended tactical roles.

segments.summary: A larger Free French fleet raises two unresolved questions: whether its support infrastructure would have followed, and how its destroyers would have performed in their intended roles.
